meta.title: She Vibes — 66 Days of AI Learning

days.title: Onboarding
days.theme: Welcome to She Vibes. Community agreement, tool setup, the She Vibes philosophy. Why this cohort exists.
days.lesson:
Why this cohort exists:

Every day a new AI tool launches. Every week someone tells you that everything has changed. And you are sitting there thinking — where do I even start?

That overwhelm is real. It is also a signal. It means you care. It means you know something important is happening and you do not want to be left behind.

She Vibes exists for exactly that moment.

This is not a course where you memorise prompts and follow templates. A colouring book never made an artist. We are not here to give you fish every day. We are here to teach you how to fish — with AI, using your own thinking, in your own life.

What you are signing up for:

66 days. One idea at a time. Every day, a small byte of learning. Every Sunday, we come together as a community for one hour to reflect, synthesise, and grow.

Think of it like this: right now, everybody uses AI the way everybody uses Excel. You open it, you get value out of it, you close it. But only a small percentage of people know how to use it at full potential — to write a formula, build a pivot table, make it work for them. We are moving you from casual user to confident practitioner. Someone who knows why something works, not just that it does.

By day 66, you will not know everything. Nobody does. But you will know how to think with AI. That is the skill that compounds forever.
days.whyItMatters:
The Three Zones of She Vibes:

Think.
This is where your value lives. AI cannot think for you. It can only think with you — and only as well as you direct it.

Do.
AI has largely taken over execution. It writes faster, codes faster, formats faster. We will use this, not fight it.

Articulate.
AI can express your ideas clearly — when you give it the right context. Learning to give context is learning to articulate what you actually want.

She Vibes focuses on the Think zone. Everything else follows from there.
days.buildTask:
The Learning Contract:

Before day 2 begins, read this and agree to it.

One: show up daily.
Each day unlocks one idea. You can read past days but you cannot submit reflections for missed days. The discipline is the point.

Two: reflect honestly.
Your submission is not for Karthi to grade. It is for you to think out loud. There are no wrong answers. There is only thinking or not thinking.

Three: Sundays are sacred.
Every Sunday we regroup for one hour as a community. This is where the real learning surfaces — from your reflections, from the group's patterns, from questions that deserve a proper answer.

Four: first come, first served.
Each day, three people get their work reviewed live. If you want that, submit early and raise your hand.

Five: the community is part of the curriculum.
220 women are doing this alongside you. Some are beginners. Some know more. All of them are here to grow. Treat every reflection shared in the group as a gift.

You have wholeheartedly accepted the learning contract.

days.title: It's Not Magic. It's Math.
days.theme: Everything AI does is math. 70 years of research. Stop fearing it, start understanding it.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Everything you see AI do today — write an email, generate an image, answer a question, write code — is the result of seventy years of mathematics built by millions of scientists across the world. It is not a genie. It is not magic. It is a very sophisticated pattern-matching engine that predicts the next most likely word, pixel, or token. That's it. And once you understand that, you stop being afraid of it.
days.whyItMatters: When AI gives you a wrong answer confidently, it's not lying to you — it's doing math that went slightly off. When you understand that, you can fix it instead of feeling fooled by it.
days.buildTask: Open any AI tool you use — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, doesn't matter. Ask it: "Explain to me how you work, like I'm a curious ten-year-old." Then ask a follow-up: "Where are you most likely to get things wrong, and why?" Share one thing that surprised you on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You now know AI is pattern-matching, not magic. So here is your challenge: find one moment this week where you caught AI being wrong — a confident mistake, an odd phrasing, an answer that felt off. Screenshot it. Then ask AI why it got it wrong. Share what it said. This is not a gotcha exercise. It is calibration. The people who use AI best are the ones who know its failure modes as well as its strengths.
days.reflectionPrompt: What's one thing you believed about AI before today that feels different now?
days.myReflection: I have been thinking that AI is kind of a customised google search engine. So Instead of googling you ask any question and it will fetch the relevant answer. But I was totally wrong. After today's build I clearly understood that AI is a super smart pattern matching engine. It's job is to predict the next best word, then next and thereby creating a helpful answer and all that is done in a fraction of a second. It has been trained with lots of lots of text so it creates a pattern. Like a kid learn the language from us, similarly it learns how words go together and learns the language. It doesn't have any feeling, emotions or it doesn't think like how we humans do. So whatever AI is generating we need to double check. We also need to understand where AI can go wrong. It can generate incorrect answers confidently.

days.title: The Seventy Year Journey
days.theme: From perceptrons in the 1950s to transformers today. The winters, the breakthroughs, the moment everything changed.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

AI didn't appear overnight. It started in the 1950s with simple models called perceptrons that could barely tell a circle from a square. Then came the AI winters — decades where funding dried up because the technology just wasn't working. Then breakthroughs: neural networks in the 80s, deep learning in the 2010s, transformers in 2017, and ChatGPT in 2022 — which put everything into the hands of ordinary people. You are living at the peak of seventy years of stubbornness and curiosity.
days.whyItMatters: When you know the history, you understand why AI feels like it arrived suddenly — it didn't. It was being built quietly for decades. And knowing that makes you trust it more intelligently, not blindly.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI tool: "Give me a timeline of the five most important moments in AI history, and explain why each one mattered." Then ask: "What do you think comes next in the next five years?" Screenshot the answer and share it on WhatsApp with your reaction.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

AI took 70 years to reach your phone. Think about one skill or craft in your own life — cooking, writing, managing people, designing — that took years to compound quietly before it clicked. Open an AI tool and have a conversation about that journey. Ask it: "How does the way humans develop expertise compare to how AI models are trained?" Then write two sentences: what's similar, and what's different. You'll understand both better by the end.
days.reflectionPrompt: Which moment in AI history surprised you the most — and why?

days.title: How AI Actually Reads You
days.theme: Tokens, embeddings, vectors. When you type a sentence, AI sees numbers. Why context and punctuation matter.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

When you type a sentence to an AI, it doesn't see words the way you do. It breaks your sentence into small chunks called tokens — sometimes a whole word, sometimes just part of one. It then converts each token into a number, and that number lives inside a vast mathematical space called an embedding. Words that mean similar things live close together in that space. "Cat" and "kitten" are neighbours. "Cat" and "invoice" are far apart. This is how AI understands meaning — not through dictionaries, but through mathematical proximity.
days.whyItMatters: This is why punctuation matters, why rephrasing a prompt can get you a completely different answer, and why longer, more specific prompts often work better. You're not typing to a person — you're navigating a mathematical space with words.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI tool: "What is tokenisation and show me how you would break this sentence into tokens: 'She vibes with AI every single day.'" Then ask: "Why does rephrasing a prompt change your answer?" Share what you learned on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You know AI sees tokens, not words. Now test it in your own work context. Take a paragraph you wrote recently — an email, a message, a document — and paste it into the OpenAI tokeniser linked above. Count the tokens. Then rewrite the same paragraph more concisely and count again. Now ask Claude or ChatGPT: "Which version of this paragraph will give you better context to respond to?" You're starting to think like a prompt engineer.
days.reflectionPrompt: Does knowing AI reads numbers instead of words change how you'll write prompts going forward?
days.myReflection: Today's build helped me to understand tokenization. AI understands numbers and not words. Any question that we ask an LLM, it's just split the sentence into multiple chunks called tokens. Then it assigns a unique number for all the tokens. Spaces and punctuations are all considered as token. Then what happens next is all the math. It generates the next best word based on the probability. So AI just understands numbers. The more detailed question we ask then it will navigate to different parts inside the modal and thus we get a answer that is useful. Explain definition and explain in simple words both have different token and different context so the output will be slightly different for both. Prompting is like programming to get the best desired Ouput.

days.title: The Prediction Machine
days.theme: Next token prediction, softmax, probability distributions. Why AI hallucinates — it's guessing, not lying.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Here is the single most important thing to understand about how AI generates text: it is predicting the next most likely token, one at a time. Every single word you see in an AI response is the result of a calculation — given everything said so far, what word comes next? There is a mathematical function called softmax that turns a huge list of possible next words into probabilities. The AI picks from those probabilities. That's it. No understanding. No feelings. Pure prediction.
days.whyItMatters: This is exactly why AI hallucinates. It isn't lying — it is confidently predicting what words should come next, even when it has run out of real knowledge to draw from. Once you understand this, you stop being shocked when it makes things up, and you start knowing when to verify.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Explain next-token prediction to me like I've never heard of it. Then give me an example where this prediction process goes wrong — a hallucination — and explain why it happened mathematically." Share the hallucination example on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

AI hallucinates because it predicts. You have intuition that also sometimes predicts wrong. Think of one domain in your work or life where you make quick calls based on pattern recognition — reading a room, estimating a timeline, judging a person's mood from a message. Ask AI: "Help me build a checklist to verify my instinct in [that domain] before I act on it." Compare how you handle your own uncertainty versus how AI should handle its uncertainty. The insight here is about knowing when to pause and verify — in yourself and in the tool.
days.reflectionPrompt: Now that you know AI is predicting word by word — does that change how much you trust it? What will you verify from now on?
days.myReflection: Yes, AI is a prediction engine. Its job is to predict the next best word given with all the information we provide. After learning more about how AI works I understood that we cannot trust it blindly. It doesn't check facts or truth. It also has a cut-off date so it won't have recent information. Sometimes AI can confidently share incorrect information which is called hallucinations. AI output is based on probability. So if it can't find a correct answer then it will fill in with the nearest possible answer. So we need to verify the answer that it generated.

referenceLinks.text: How Large Language Models Work — Stephen Wolfram

days.title: Training, Fine-tuning, and You
days.theme: Pretraining, RLHF, posttraining. How the model learned everything. You've been part of training AI.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Before AI can predict anything, it has to learn. This happens in stages. First, pretraining — the model reads a vast portion of the internet and learns the patterns of human language. This takes months and costs millions. Then fine-tuning — the model is shaped to be helpful and safe, using human feedback. Real people rated responses as good or bad, and those ratings taught the model how to behave. This process is called RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Every thumbs up and thumbs down you've ever given an AI has been part of training future models.
days.whyItMatters: You are not just a user of AI. You have been — without knowing it — a contributor to how it thinks. And understanding this helps you see AI not as an oracle, but as a mirror of human knowledge, with all its biases and blind spots included.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Explain the difference between pretraining and fine-tuning. What kind of biases could creep in during each stage?" Then ask: "What is RLHF and how did human feedback shape how you respond?" Reflect on one bias you've noticed in AI responses and share it on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

AI was fine-tuned on human feedback. You've been fine-tuned by your experiences too. Think of one strong professional opinion you hold — about how meetings should run, how feedback should be given, how projects get done. Ask AI the same question and compare its answer to yours. Then ask: "What life experiences or data might have shaped your answer differently from mine?" You're reverse-engineering bias in AI and in yourself simultaneously. That's the most human use of AI I can think of.
days.reflectionPrompt: If AI learned from human feedback — what do you think it learned about how women communicate, ask questions, and seek help?
days.myReflection: Today's build helped me to understand how model was trained. Basically there are pre-training, fine tuning and RLHF. Pre-training is basically the entire internet is feed into the AI. Now with pre-training AI can be raw and it could be dangerous. We need to fine tune the system. Fine tuning helps AI to give structured, helpful and safe answers to us. Example if you ask to generate test cases it will generate in a structured output. Finally AI will learn from human feedback which is called Reinforcement learning with human feedback. Asking a question and AI will generate two different answers. A human has to select the best appropriate answer and the model will learn from human feedback.

referenceLinks.text: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — Anthropic

days.title: The Layers You Never See
days.theme: From raw model to chat interface. APIs, wrappers, products built on top. Claude and ChatGPT are interfaces — underneath is math.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

When you open ChatGPT or Claude, you're not talking directly to the raw AI model. You're talking through layers. At the bottom is the foundation model — billions of parameters, trained on vast data. On top of that sits a system prompt, invisible to you, that shapes how the AI behaves. On top of that is the API — a way for software to talk to the model programmatically, without any chat interface at all. And finally, the product layer — the chat window you actually see. Strip away all those layers and the math still runs. AI can work even when the friendly interface is gone. This is the world you're about to build in.
days.whyItMatters: Understanding the layers means you understand what's possible. The chat interface is just one way to interact with AI. Apps, automations, agents — they all bypass the chat window and talk directly to the API. This week planted the seed. The coming weeks will show you how to build on top of these layers yourself.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Explain the difference between a foundation model, an API, and a chat interface. If I wanted to build my own app using you as the brain — which layer would I be working with?" Then ask: "What is a system prompt and what can it do?" Share your biggest 'aha' from Week 1 on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You now know there are layers between you and the AI. Here's your challenge: think of one tool you use at work or at home that you suspect has AI built in somewhere underneath — an email client, a writing tool, a search bar, a customer support chat. Ask the AI: "Does [tool name] use an AI model? What layer of the stack is the AI operating at?" Then ask: "If I wanted to customise how it behaves, what layer would I need to access?" You're starting to see the world as a stack, not a black box.
days.reflectionPrompt: Looking back at the whole week — what is the one thing that most changed how you see AI?
days.myReflection: Before joining the cohort my understanding about AI is that it's a super smart machine which answers whatever I ask. It knows everything and we can just rely on AI for everything. ChatGPT or claude you can use any AI and get things done as quickly as possible. But gradually my perspectives changed about AI. Its a prediction engine. Its job is to predict the next best token based on everything it knows. It's a big mathematical function. It is able to give you helpful answers because it was trained on vast data, almost everything on the internet. So it is able to understand how language works and how words go together. It's able to pattern matching. Also human feedback is added to AI. Humans helped the model to give thumbs up and down based on the response it provided. It's rewarded for answers that are helpful. Even if the answer is not true but AI will confidently say it because it's the probability and the pattern so it decides based on the probability. So there could be a wrong answer but AI says confidently which is called hallucinations. AI can also be biased because if the training data is biased or if the human who gave feedback can also be biased. Hence the AI is also biased. It's always necessary that we need to validate it's answers. AI doesn't know everything and it doesn't know if it doesn't know anything.

days.title: Reflection: Week 1
days.theme: What shifted in how you see AI this week? Share one before/after on WhatsApp.
days.lesson:
This week's arc:

You started not knowing what was underneath the chat window. By now you know: tokens, embeddings, next-token prediction, softmax, pretraining, RLHF, APIs, system prompts. You didn't just learn vocabulary — you built a mental model. AI is no longer a black box. It's a very sophisticated prediction machine built on seventy years of human curiosity.

Looking ahead:

Next week is Prompt Engineering. You now understand what AI is under the hood. Next week you learn how to talk to it — properly. How to ask for exactly what you want. How to debug when it gets it wrong. How to make it work harder for you.

See you Monday.
days.whyItMatters: Week 1 complete. You built a mental model of AI from scratch. Next week: Prompt Engineering — how to talk to AI properly.

days.reflectionPrompt: Before She Vibes Week 1, I thought AI was __. Now I know it's __.
days.myReflection:
Before joining this cohort, I had this idea about AI where it is kind of an advanced Google search engine. If you ask any question, it gives you a smart reply and it would answer any question that you want to ask. I thought it is a perfect machine because it is almost giving you perfect answers, so that is going to be the only thing where humans are going to ask any questions moving forward. It is also going to take us all over a job in the future, so that's what my thinking about AI, or my perspective about AI, before I joined this cohort.

After one week of learning AI byte by byte every day, now I understand that AI is kind of a prediction engine. It can only predict based on some mathematical function and probability, so it is all based on some training, because it had got some pre-training, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from humans. It is going to give you answers, or you can tell; it is going to predict what should be the next word. Because of this, it could also hallucinate, meaning even though it doesn't know the truth, it can confidently say that this is what it is, so that's hallucination. There are a lot of things going behind this. For example, you write a question that you asked, and it is just converting that to tokens and then it is converting it to numbers called embeddings. It goes through a huge list of vocabulary, or you can call it a map of words, and a lot of mathematical functions behind the scenes. It is going to predict the next word given whatever that you said so far to it, so it's kind of a prediction engine.

You cannot rely on everything for an AI. You need to be mindful of where the AI can fail and where the AI can give you good results so that you can use it according to your application or according to your use cases. That perspective had changed; earlier I used to have a fear of AI, but right now I'm confident because I know, at the foundation level, what this AI is doing. Now I'm confident about how I should use this AI and what it does when I ask the AI a question, so that has totally changed. I'm also trying to understand and explore more how I can effectively or efficiently use the AI for all my day-to-day work. One thing is for sure: my perspective totally changed on AI from a super smart, super smart question-answer to kind of a more just a prediction machine, I would say.

days.title: What is a Prompt?
days.theme: A prompt is an instruction, a conversation, a specification. The quality of your output starts here.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

A prompt is simply what you say to AI to get it to do something. But that's like saying a recipe is just words on a page. The quality of your prompt determines everything — the clarity of the answer, the usefulness of the output, whether you feel like AI is working with you or against you. Most people type the first thing that comes to mind. Skilled prompters think like designers: what do I actually want, who do I want AI to be, and what context does it need to help me well?
days.whyItMatters: The gap between a mediocre AI response and an exceptional one is almost always the prompt. The model hasn't changed. The question has.
days.buildTask: Pick one real task from your life — a work email, a plan, a problem you're thinking about. Write the first prompt that comes to mind and see what you get. Then rewrite it with more specificity and context. Compare the two responses. Share both prompts and both responses on WhatsApp with your observation.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You compared two prompts today. Now go further. Take the same task and write five different versions of the prompt — each one adding a different element: role, tone, format, constraint, example. Run all five. Notice which dimension made the biggest difference for your specific use case. Then write a one-line "prompt formula" for this type of task that you'll reuse. You're building your own prompt library, personalised to your work and life.
days.reflectionPrompt: What was different between your first prompt and your second? What did adding context actually change?
days.myReflection: So, for today's learning, I picked up a use case in my day-to-day work. I asked a generic prompt to the AI, and it gave me an average output. I just tweaked my prompt to how I want the AI to act like and then I added some specificity, like I gave context, I gave instruction, I gave the output format. Then it gave me a detailed answer, which is very helpful. I understood that the quality of my output is based on the prompt. I need to design my prompt in such way that has more details and specificity. I should have a Role, Context, Problem statement, Instruction, output format.

days.title: Simple Prompts That Work
days.theme: Clear, specific, direct. The anatomy of a prompt that gets results. Practice with everyday tasks.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

You don't need complex frameworks to get good results from AI. You need clarity. The three ingredients of a prompt that works are: be specific about what you want, tell it the format you want it in, and give it enough context to actually help you. That's it. "Write me an email" is weak. "Write a short, warm email to my manager explaining I'll be 30 minutes late to tomorrow's 10am meeting, and suggest we push it to 10:30" is strong. Same task. Completely different result.
days.whyItMatters: Most people give up on AI too early because their vague prompts get vague responses. Specificity is the single biggest lever you have. Pull it.
days.buildTask: Take three everyday tasks — something you'd normally do yourself — and write one prompt for each that is specific, gives context, and asks for a clear format. Try: a message to a friend, a to-do list for your week, a summary of something you read recently. Share your three prompts and the outputs on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Simple prompts work for simple tasks. Now stress-test the principle. Find the most complex, annoying, recurring task in your work week — the one that takes you the longest and feels the most draining. Write the most specific, context-rich prompt you can for it. Run it. If the output isn't good enough, don't give up — ask AI: "What additional information would you need from me to do this better?" This is how you build a prompt that you'll actually reuse every week.
days.reflectionPrompt: Which of your three prompts got the best result — and what made it work?
days.myReflection:
All my 3 tasks gave me a good output. These are simple tasks which I do everyday. It gave me a detailed output but if I follow it that may confuse my team. I need to reiterate this by giving examples of how I'm doing it everyday now so that it can understand and give more feedback.

1. Create a to-do list for my day to day work. As a QA engineer I will understand what work I need to get done morning and I will prepare a to-do list so that I won't miss anything. Create a effective to-do list.

2. I want you to create a template or a framework for posting my daily work status updates. We have a onshore and offshore team. So at the end of the day I need post my work updates to onshore team. Give me a clear template where I can post it and convey the same updates in evening stand-up. Keep it clear and clarity.

3. I want you to act as an experienced scrum master who can run daily stand-ups. My team don't have a scrum master so it's getting messed up daily morning. I want you to tell me how would you run a standup effectively. I need step by step detail on what would say first thing once everyone joined and things like that.

referenceLinks.text: Be clear and direct — Anthropic Prompting Guide

days.title: Role, Context, Task
days.theme: The three-part prompt framework. Tell AI who it is, what it knows, what you need. See the difference.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

The most reliable prompt structure you'll ever use has three parts. First, the role — tell AI who to be. "Act as a senior product manager" or "You are a warm, experienced coach." This shapes the tone, expertise, and perspective of everything that follows. Second, the context — tell it what it needs to know. Your situation, constraints, what's already happened. Third, the task — tell it exactly what to do. When you combine all three, AI stops being a search engine and starts being a thinking partner.
days.whyItMatters: Role shapes voice. Context shapes relevance. Task shapes output. Miss any one of the three and the response feels generic. Nail all three and it feels like it was written for you — because it was.
days.buildTask: Write one prompt using all three parts for something meaningful in your life right now. Example: "You are an experienced career coach who specialises in women in tech. I've been in my current role for two years and I feel like I'm not growing. I have a 1:1 with my manager tomorrow. Write me five questions I can ask to open a conversation about my growth path." Share your prompt and response on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You've used Role-Context-Task once. Now build a reusable version for your most common AI use case. Think about the single thing you use AI for most — writing, planning, research, feedback. Write a "master prompt" in Role-Context-Task format that you can paste at the start of any conversation on that topic. This becomes your personal system prompt — your AI's default mode of working with you. Save it somewhere you'll actually use it.
days.reflectionPrompt: How did adding a role change the tone of the response? Would you have written it differently yourself?
days.myReflection:
Adding a role changed the entire response and AI gives more contextual answer. My first prompt was around acting as a QA architect and asked solution for a problem and it did gave me top 3 suggestions that are helpful. When I removes the role from the prompt and it did generate a totally different response and the response structure also changed.

days.title: When It Gets It Wrong
days.theme: Debugging your prompts. When AI fails, it's information. How to iterate, refine, and fix.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

AI will get things wrong. It will misunderstand your question, give you something too generic, go off in the wrong direction, or simply make something up. This is not a failure — it's information. Every bad response tells you something about what your prompt was missing. The skill isn't writing a perfect prompt the first time. The skill is knowing how to read a bad response and iterate. Did it misunderstand your context? Did it take the wrong tone? Was it too long, too short, too formal? Each of these has a fix.
days.whyItMatters: The people who get the most out of AI are not the ones who write perfect prompts. They're the ones who aren't afraid to push back, refine, and ask again. Iteration is the skill. One-shot is the myth.
days.buildTask: Intentionally write a vague or incomplete prompt on a topic you care about. Get the response. Then diagnose what went wrong and rewrite the prompt to fix it. Do this twice with two different topics. Share your "before and after" prompts on WhatsApp with a one-line diagnosis of what changed.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Debugging AI is a skill. So is debugging yourself. Find a decision you made recently at work or at home that didn't go the way you wanted. Describe it to AI and ask: "Based on what I've told you, what information was I missing when I made this decision, and what questions should I have asked myself first?" Then ask: "If you were advising me at the time, what would you have said?" You're using AI to debug your thinking the same way you debug a prompt.

5. Output format or structure.

days.title: Complex Prompts for Complex Tasks
days.theme: Chaining prompts, multi-step instructions, system prompts. Building workflows through language.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Some tasks are too big for a single prompt. A report, a plan, a multi-step analysis — these need a different approach. Chaining is the technique of breaking a big task into smaller prompts where each output feeds the next. First, ask AI to think through the problem. Then ask it to structure the solution. Then ask it to write it. You can also use a single long prompt with numbered steps — tell AI exactly what to do in sequence. The key insight is that AI doesn't get tired. You can have a long, structured conversation and build something substantial, one step at a time.
days.whyItMatters: One long, overwhelming prompt produces one mediocre response. A sequence of focused prompts — each building on the last — produces something genuinely useful. This is how you build with AI, not just chat with it.
days.buildTask: Pick a complex task you've been putting off — a plan, a proposal, a difficult message, a strategy. Break it into at least three sequential prompts. Run them one after another, letting each response inform the next. Share your final output on WhatsApp and describe your prompt chain.

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Write the full sequence of prompts you'd use to AI-assist that process from start to finish. You don't need to run them all today. Just write the chain. This is the beginning of building your own AI workflow — a repeatable, improvable process that compounds every time you use it.

days.title: Prompting Across Tools
days.theme: Same principles, different tools. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot — how to be tool-agnostic.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

The prompting principles you've learned this week work everywhere. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity — they all respond to the same fundamentals: be specific, give context, assign a role, iterate. The differences between tools are real but secondary. Claude tends to be more thoughtful and nuanced. ChatGPT is fast and versatile. Gemini is deeply connected to Google's ecosystem. Perplexity is excellent for research with live sources. Knowing the strengths of each means you can pick the right tool for the right job — and your prompting skills transfer instantly.
days.whyItMatters: You are not learning how to use one tool. You are learning how to think with AI. That skill is durable. Tools will change. Your ability to prompt well will not.

days.title: What is Context?
days.theme: Context windows, memory, and why AI forgets. The more relevant context you give, the better it performs.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

AI only knows what you tell it. Within a single conversation, it remembers everything you've said — but the moment you start a new conversation, it forgets all of it. This is called the context window. Think of it like a whiteboard that gets wiped clean every session. The size of that whiteboard varies by model — some can hold a few thousand words, others can hold entire books. The more relevant information you put on that whiteboard, the better AI performs. Context engineering is the practice of filling that whiteboard deliberately.
days.whyItMatters: Most people talk to AI like it already knows them. It doesn't. Every conversation starts fresh. The people who get the most out of AI are the ones who bring the right context every time — who they are, what they're working on, what they've already tried, what good looks like.
days.buildTask: Start a new conversation with any AI tool and give it zero context. Ask it to help you with something specific in your life. See what you get. Then start a fresh conversation and spend three sentences giving it full context before asking the same question. Compare the two responses. Share both on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Write your personal context block — a 10-line description of who you are, what you do, how you think, and what you use AI for. This is your personal system prompt. Every time you start a new AI conversation about your work or life, paste this at the top. Over the next week, notice how the quality of your interactions changes. Refine the block each time something feels missing. This is the beginning of your personal AI operating layer.

days.title: Connecting AI to Your World
days.theme: APIs, integrations, connectors. How AI reaches beyond its training to your actual data.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

The chat window is the smallest version of what AI can do. In the real world, AI doesn't have to wait for you to type information — it can go and fetch it. This is done through APIs. An API is a door between two pieces of software. When AI is connected to an API, it can reach into your calendar, your email, your documents, your databases — and bring that information into the conversation automatically. You stop being the one who has to remember and relay everything. The AI does that for you.
days.whyItMatters: This is the shift from AI as a chat tool to AI as a working partner. The moment it has access to your actual world — your actual data, your actual context — it stops giving generic answers and starts giving answers that are specific to your situation.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "What is an API? Give me three examples of how an AI connected to APIs could help someone in my kind of work — give me specific, concrete use cases, not abstract ones." Pick the use case that excites you most and describe what your life would look like if that existed. Share it on WhatsApp.

Draw it on paper, in Notion, or describe it in a voice memo. Then ask AI: "Help me design this workflow in detail. What would I need to set up to make this real today?" You may be surprised how close you already are.

days.title: What is an MCP?
days.theme: Model Context Protocol. How AI connects to live tools — your calendar, email, files. The magic of real-time context.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is a standard — a common language — that lets AI connect to tools and data sources in a structured, reliable way. Think of it as a universal adapter. Before MCP, every integration between AI and a tool was custom-built and fragile. With MCP, an AI can connect to your Notion, your Gmail, your calendar, your GitHub — using the same protocol each time. This is what makes it possible for AI to look at your emails and say "here are the three things you need to act on today" — without you copying and pasting anything.
days.whyItMatters: MCP is one of the most important infrastructure shifts happening in AI right now. It is what makes AI genuinely useful in your daily work — not just as a chat tool, but as something that knows your context and acts on it. Understanding it now puts you ahead.
days.buildTask: Open Claude at claude.ai and look at the connectors available in the left panel. Connect one — Notion, Google Drive, or whatever you use. Then ask Claude: "What are the most important things I should pay attention to today based on what you can see?" Share what it found — and your reaction — on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You connected AI to one tool today. Now go further. Connect a second tool and ask Claude to reason across both. For example: connect your calendar and your email, then ask: "Based on my meetings this week and my unread emails, what should my priorities be today?" This is AI as a chief of staff, not just a chat window. Notice what it gets right and what it misses. That gap is your next prompt engineering challenge.
days.reflectionPrompt: What was it like having AI look at your actual data instead of imagined data? What surprised you?

That was great, because if I had to do this manually, I have to go open, log in to Gmail, go to the inbox, and read the emails one by one, which is going to be time-consuming. AI made it very easy, and thanks to MCP, it connected to my Gmail and calendar and listed out all the emails that need my attention, and it was so easy.

days.title: Building Your First Integration
days.theme: Connect AI to one tool you already use. See what becomes possible when context flows freely.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Today you stop reading about integrations and build one. An integration is simply two tools talking to each other. The simplest integrations use something called a webhook — a way for one tool to send a message to another whenever something happens. More powerful integrations use Zapier or Make, which let you connect hundreds of tools without writing a single line of code. The principle is always the same: when this happens in tool A, do that in tool B. AI can sit in the middle — receiving the data, doing something intelligent with it, and sending a result back.
days.whyItMatters: This is the moment AI stops being a chat window and becomes infrastructure. One working integration — even a simple one — changes how you think about what's possible. It makes the abstract concrete.
days.buildTask: Go to Zapier (zapier.com) and create a free account. You don't need AI in it yet — just connect two tools and make something happen automatically. Share a screenshot of your working Zap on WhatsApp.

Ask it to summarise, classify, or extract something useful from the data before it hits tool B. For example: email arrives — AI extracts the action item — action item is added to your task list. You've just built an AI-powered workflow. That's not a future thing. You just did it.

days.title: Context in Practice
days.theme: Real use cases: AI that reads your emails, summarises your day, knows your projects. Build one for yourself.

The Idea:

Let's make this real. Today is about building a context-rich AI workflow for your actual daily life. What needs your attention, what can wait, what decision is coming that you should be thinking about. This is what becomes possible when AI has context. days.title: RAG and Beyond
days.theme: Retrieval Augmented Generation. How AI can search your own documents. The future of personal AI.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation. It sounds technical but the idea is simple: instead of relying only on what the AI learned during training, you give it access to a specific set of documents — your documents — and it retrieves the relevant ones before answering your question. This is how you build an AI that knows your company's policies, your personal notes, your research library, your product documentation. You ask a question, it searches your documents, it answers based on what it finds. No more "I don't have access to that information."
days.whyItMatters: RAG is what closes the gap between generic AI and your AI. It is the technology behind tools like NotebookLM, Perplexity, and any AI that can answer questions about your specific content. Understanding it means you can choose and use these tools intelligently — and eventually build with them.

days.title: What is an AI Agent?
days.theme: Agents are AI that acts, not just answers. Autonomous, repeatable, scalable. The shift from tool to colleague.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

An AI agent is not a chatbot. A chatbot waits for you to ask something, answers, and stops. An agent acts. It has a goal, a set of tools it can use, and the ability to make decisions about what to do next — without you guiding every step. You say "research the top five competitors in my market and send me a summary by 9am." The agent searches the web, reads pages, synthesises findings, writes the summary, and sends it. You were asleep. It was working. This is the shift from AI as a tool you operate to AI as a colleague you delegate to.
days.whyItMatters: The people who will get the most from AI in the next five years are not the ones who prompt best. They are the ones who delegate best. Knowing how to set up an agent — what goal to give it, what tools to equip it with, when to trust it and when to check — is the new management skill.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Explain what an AI agent is, how it differs from a regular chatbot, and give me three concrete examples of agents that could help someone in my kind of work. Be specific — not generic." Then think of one repetitive task in your life that you'd love to never do again. Describe it on WhatsApp.

Stretch — go further if you are ready

You identified the task you'd hand off. Now write the agent brief for it — as if you were briefing a new team member. What is the goal? What information does the agent need? What tools should it have access to? What does a good output look like? What should it not do? The discipline of writing a clear agent brief is the same discipline as writing a clear job description or delegation note. Ask AI to review your brief and tell you what's missing. This is the thinking skill that separates good delegators from great ones.

So 4 people spend their time for 2 days to analyse the report. This can be delegated to AI. AI can do a wonderful job is analysing the report and come up with pass and fail percentage. Help team in AI adoption. Try to identify gaps in requirements, process improvements.

days.title: How Agents Work
days.theme: Planning, tools, memory, action loops. The anatomy of an agent that works while you sleep.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Under the hood, every agent runs a loop. It receives a goal. It makes a plan. It picks a tool — search, write, send, calculate, read a file. It takes an action. It looks at the result. It decides what to do next. It loops until the goal is achieved or it gets stuck and asks for help. This is called the ReAct loop — Reason, Act, Observe, repeat. The tools available to an agent determine what it can do. Give it access to your calendar and it can schedule. Give it access to your email and it can draft and send. Give it access to the web and it can research. The more tools, the more capable.
days.whyItMatters: Once you understand the loop, you understand the limits. Agents are not magic — they are structured reasoning plus tool access. They get confused when goals are vague, when tools fail, or when context runs out. Knowing this makes you a better agent designer, not just an agent user.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Walk me through the ReAct loop step by step using this example: I ask you to find the best free project management tool for a solo freelancer and send me a comparison table by email. What exactly would you do at each step?" Share the most interesting step in the reasoning on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You understand the ReAct loop now. Replay a real work situation through it. Think of a complex task you did last week — a decision, a piece of research, a plan you wrote. Map out what you did using the Reason-Act-Observe loop: what did you reason about, what action did you take, what did you observe, what did you do next? Then ask AI to do the same task using the same loop. Compare the two paths. Where did your human reasoning diverge from AI's? That divergence is where your judgment lives.
days.reflectionPrompt: Where in the agent's reasoning loop would you most want to stay in control — and where would you happily let it run on its own?
days.myReflection:
An agent will work based on ReAct framework. It can do reason, act, observe and decide. This will happen in loop until the goal is reached. Let's take an example of test report analysis.

Agent will do this in 6 steps.

Loop 1 — Understanding the goal

Loop 2 — Reading the reports

Loop 3 — Categorising failures

Loop 4 — Calculating percentages

Loop 5 — Writing the summary

Loop 6 — Sending it out

I want to stay in control on how the agent categorise the results. It can understand, read the report but on what basis it categorise the results is very important in my opinion so I want be in control. Calculation percentages, writing detailed summary and sending it out to slack I will leave it to the agent and trust it.
referenceLinks: ReAct: Synergising reasoning and acting in language models — arXiv

days.title: Your First Agent
days.theme: Build a simple automation. Something that runs without you. Experience what autonomy feels like.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

The simplest agent you can build today is an automated workflow that takes an input, does something intelligent with it, and produces an output — without you in the middle. You don't need to write code. Tools like Zapier, Make, and n8n let you connect apps and add an AI step that reasons about the data flowing through. The result is a mini-agent: something that runs on a trigger, thinks, and acts. It might not be sophisticated. But it will be yours — and the feeling of watching it work the first time is the moment everything becomes real.
days.whyItMatters: Your first agent will be simple. That is exactly the point. Every sophisticated automation you'll ever build starts with one trigger, one AI step, one output. The complexity comes later. The habit starts today.
days.buildTask: Go back to Zapier (or Make if you prefer). Build a workflow with at least one AI step. The simplest version: when you add a row to a Google Sheet with a task description, have AI generate a one-paragraph brief for that task and send it to you by email or Slack. You are the one who triggers it — AI is the one who does the thinking. Share a screenshot of your working workflow on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

Your first agent runs. Now stress-test it. Give it five different inputs — vary the task description, the complexity, the length. Watch how the AI step handles each one. Where does it do well? Where does it produce generic or weak output? Now go back and improve the AI prompt inside your Zap based on what you learned. You're not just building an agent — you're iterating on it. That iteration instinct is the most important engineering habit you'll develop in She Vibes.
days.reflectionPrompt: What did it feel like to watch an automated workflow run without you doing the work? What does that unlock?
days.myReflection: It's great to see the automated workflow. My use case is simple. I want AI to send me a list of a summary of the tech emails I have received. It will give me a brief and summarise and send it to my email. I used zapier do create a 4 step workflow. Everyday 8 am, the summary of tech blogs will reach my email. I don't need to look into all emails instead just read the summary. This unlocks that I can automate workflows that is repetitive and don't need manual intervention. Once set it up and it will run everyday.

days.title: Agent Use Cases
days.theme: Content agents, research agents, scheduling agents. Map real problems in your life to agent solutions.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Agents are not one thing. They take different shapes depending on the job. A content agent monitors topics you care about, pulls new articles daily, and delivers a curated digest. A research agent takes a question, searches the web, reads sources, and produces a structured report. A scheduling agent looks at your calendar and email, finds the best meeting slots, and drafts the invite. A customer support agent reads incoming messages, classifies them, drafts responses, and escalates the ones it can't handle. All of these exist today. All of them are within your reach to use — and within your reach to build.
days.whyItMatters: The question is never "does an agent exist for this?" It's "what is the goal, what are the inputs, what are the outputs, and what decisions need to happen in between?" Once you can frame any problem that way, you can design an agent for it.
days.buildTask: Map three agent use cases from your own life using this format for each: Goal — Trigger — Input — AI step — Output — Who it helps. They don't have to be built yet. Just mapped clearly. Share your three use cases on WhatsApp. The most specific one wins.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You mapped three use cases. Now pick the one that saves you the most time and actually build it — even a rough version. Use Zapier, Make, or Claude with connected tools. It doesn't have to be perfect. It has to run once, end to end. Then document what it does in two sentences and what you'd improve next. Share that documentation on WhatsApp. A rough working agent beats a perfect unbuilt one every time.
days.reflectionPrompt: Of your three use cases — which one, if it existed today, would save you the most time or mental energy every single week?

days.title: Multi-Agent Systems
days.theme: Agents that talk to agents. Orchestration, handoffs, specialisation. The autonomous workforce explained.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

One agent can do a lot. But some tasks are too complex for one agent alone — they need a team. A multi-agent system is exactly that: multiple agents, each with a specialised role, working together on a shared goal. An orchestrator agent receives the goal and breaks it into sub-tasks. It delegates each sub-task to a specialist agent — one for research, one for writing, one for checking facts, one for formatting. Each does its job, returns the result, and the orchestrator assembles the final output. This is not science fiction. It is how some of today's most powerful AI workflows already operate.
days.whyItMatters: This is the future of knowledge work. Not one AI doing everything, but a coordinated team of agents — each expert in its lane — working in parallel while you focus on the goal, not the execution. Understanding this now means you can think about your own work in terms of specialisation, delegation, and orchestration.
days.buildTask: Ask any AI: "Design a multi-agent system that could help a solo creator produce a weekly newsletter — from research to writing to proofreading to publishing. Name each agent, describe its role, and explain how they hand off to each other." Share the design on WhatsApp with your reaction.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You designed a multi-agent newsletter system. Now map one for your own life or work. What complex recurring output do you produce — a report, a strategy doc, a team update, a client pitch? Break it into its component parts. Assign a specialist agent role to each part. Draw the handoffs. Then ask AI: "Review this multi-agent design. What are the weakest handoff points? Where would this system most likely fail?" You're thinking like an AI systems architect now.
days.reflectionPrompt: If you had a team of specialist agents working for you, what would each one do — and what would you keep for yourself?
days.myReflection:
Day 27 build task completed.

Designed a multi-agent newsletter system for a solo creator:

Orchestrator Agent — receives the topic, breaks it into sub-tasks, assigns to specialist agents, assembles final output.

Agent 1 — Research Agent: Searches web, reads articles, finds top 5 relevant sources, extracts key facts and data. Hands off structured research brief to Content Agent.

Agent 2 — Content Agent: Takes research brief, writes full newsletter draft — intro, body, takeaways, call to action. Hands off raw draft to Proofreading Agent.

Agent 3 — Proofreading Agent: Checks grammar, clarity, tone, factual accuracy against research. Flags issues. Hands off corrected draft to Formatting Agent.

Agent 4 — Formatting Agent: Formats for publishing platform — headings, spacing, subject line, preview text, footer. Hands off to Publishing Agent.

Agent 5 — Publishing Agent: Connects to Substack or Beehiiv, schedules at optimal send time, sends newsletter. Confirms back to Orchestrator.

Key insight: The most critical handoff is Research to Content. If the research brief is weak, every downstream agent produces weaker output.

If I had a team of specialist agents for my QA work:
- Research Agent — reads PBIs and requirements
- Test Plan Agent — generates test cases
- Execution Agent — runs automated tests
- Analysis Agent — classifies failures and calculates percentages
- Reporting Agent — writes and sends summary to team

What I would keep for myself: The judgment call on what constitutes a real bug vs environment noise. That requires domain knowledge and accountability that no agent should own alone.

days.title: When Agents Go Wrong
days.theme: Failure modes, guardrails, human-in-the-loop. Knowing when to trust your agent and when to check.
days.lesson:
The Idea:

Agents are powerful. They are also fallible. They can misunderstand a goal and pursue it confidently in the wrong direction. They can get into loops, retrying failed steps endlessly. They can hallucinate tool outputs — believing they did something they didn't. They can make irreversible actions: sending an email, deleting a file, posting publicly. This is why the most important concept in agent design is human-in-the-loop — knowing exactly which decisions your agent should make autonomously, and which ones it should pause and ask you about first. Not all automation should run unattended. The art is knowing the difference.
days.whyItMatters: An agent without guardrails is not an assistant — it's a liability. The builders who ship reliable agents are the ones who think carefully about failure modes before they happen, not after. This is not pessimism. It is good engineering.
days.buildTask: Take the agent use case you identified on Day 26 as most valuable. Now stress-test it. Ask any AI: "Here is my agent use case: [paste it]. What are the five most likely ways this agent could go wrong? For each failure mode, suggest a guardrail." Share the failure modes and guardrails on WhatsApp.
days.stretchTask:
Stretch — push yourself further

Optional. For those who want to go beyond the byte.

You mapped failure modes for your agent. Now write its operating rules — a short list of what it should always do, never do, and always check with you before doing. Think of it as an agent constitution. Then ask AI: "Based on these rules, design the simplest possible human-in-the-loop checkpoint for this agent." A good checkpoint takes under 30 seconds of your time but prevents the five failures you just identified. That's the trade-off you're designing for.
days.reflectionPrompt: What is the one action you would never want an agent to take without checking with you first — and why?
days.myReflection: I would want the agent to pause and ask me if it needed more information to take a decision instead of assuming. At any case if agent doesn't have any information or not clear with inputs then the agent should not assume anything and do the action instead. It should always pause and ask the human instead of taking any action which could harm the user. So I would never want an agent to take any action when it's going to assume anything. I would always want the human in the loop in critical applications. We cannot fully trust agents and they can hallucinate.
referenceLinks: Building safe and reliable agents — Anthropic
